question: When choosing a motorcycle that fits you, the manual says your feet should:
choice_a: Reach the ground while you are seated on the motorcycle
choice_b: Only reach the ground when the motorcycle is tilted
choice_c: Rest comfortably above the pegs at all times
choice_d: Not need to touch the ground if you have good balance
explanation: Your motorcycle should 'fit' you: your feet should reach the ground while you are seated on the motorcycle, and the controls should be easy to operate.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.5, 'The Right Motorcycle For You'

question: The manual recommends which size of motorcycle for beginning riders?
choice_a: The largest available, for more stability
choice_b: Smaller motorcycles, which are usually easier for beginners to operate
choice_c: Any size, as long as it has a windshield
explanation: Smaller motorcycles are usually easier for beginners to operate.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.5, 'The Right Motorcycle For You'

question: According to the manual, at minimum a street-legal motorcycle should have all of the following EXCEPT:
choice_b: Front and rear brakes and two mirrors
choice_d: A passenger seat and factory windshield
explanation: At minimum, a street-legal motorcycle should have a headlight, taillight, and brakelight; front and rear brakes; turn signals; a horn; and two mirrors. A passenger seat and windshield are not listed as minimum equipment.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.5, 'Know Your Motorcycle'

question: If you borrow a motorcycle, the manual advises you to:
choice_a: Get familiar with it in a controlled area before riding it in traffic
choice_b: Ride it exactly as you would your own motorcycle
choice_c: Skip your normal pre-ride check since it isn't yours
choice_d: Only ride it at night to avoid attention
explanation: If you borrow a motorcycle, get familiar with it in a controlled area first; riding an unfamiliar motorcycle adds to the risk of a crash, especially for beginning riders.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.6, 'Borrowing and Lending'

question: Before lending your motorcycle to a friend, the manual says you should make sure they:
choice_a: Are licensed and know how to ride
choice_c: Have ridden that exact model before
explanation: If you lend your motorcycle to friends, make sure they are licensed and know how to ride before allowing them out into traffic.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.6, 'Borrowing and Lending'

question: Why does the manual say to ride extra carefully on a motorcycle that is new or unfamiliar to you, no matter how experienced you are?
choice_a: New motorcycles are mechanically less reliable
choice_b: Insurance does not cover unfamiliar motorcycles
choice_c: State law requires a break-in period
choice_d: It takes time to adjust, so you need a greater margin for errors
explanation: No matter how experienced you may be, ride extra carefully on any motorcycle that's new or unfamiliar to you -- it takes time to adjust, so give yourself a greater margin for errors.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.6, 'Borrowing and Lending'

question: Before riding an unfamiliar motorcycle, the manual says you should locate the turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel-control valve, and engine cut-off switch and:
choice_a: Have the previous owner point them out during the ride
choice_b: Photograph the control layout for reference
choice_c: Find and operate these items without having to look for them
choice_d: Cover them with tape until you're familiar with the bike
explanation: Find out where everything is on an unfamiliar motorcycle -- particularly the turn signals, horn, headlight switch, fuel-control valve, and engine cut-off switch -- and find and operate these items without having to look for them.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.6, 'Getting Familiar with the Motorcycle'

question: Before starting out on any motorcycle, the manual advises working the throttle, clutch, and brakes a few times because:
choice_a: It warms up the engine oil faster
choice_b: It is required before every legal ride
choice_c: All controls react a little differently from one motorcycle to another
explanation: Know the gear pattern and work the throttle, clutch, and brakes a few times before you start riding, since all controls react a little differently.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.6, 'Getting Familiar with the Motorcycle'

question: During a pre-ride check, checking hydraulic fluids and coolants, along with looking underneath the motorcycle for leaks, should be done:
choice_c: Only if the motorcycle is over five years old
explanation: At a minimum, check hydraulic fluids and coolants weekly, and look under the motorcycle for signs of an oil or gas leak.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.7, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: When adjusting mirrors before a ride, the manual says each mirror should be set so you can see:
choice_a: Only the license plate of the vehicle behind you
choice_b: The lane behind you and as much as possible of the lane next to you
choice_c: Only your own shoulder for a reference point
choice_d: The road directly beneath the motorcycle
explanation: Adjust each mirror so you can see the lane behind you and as much as possible of the lane next to you; a properly adjusted mirror may show the edge of your arm or shoulder, but the road behind and to the side is what matters most.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.7, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: During the pre-ride brake check, the manual says the front and rear brake levers should each:
choice_a: Feel firm and hold the motorcycle when fully applied
choice_b: Feel spongy but still stop the motorcycle eventually
choice_c: Require both hands to apply fully
choice_d: Be tested only after the ride, not before
explanation: Try the front and rear brake levers one at a time; make sure each one feels firm and holds the motorcycle when the brake is fully applied.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.7, 'Check Your Motorcycle'

question: According to the manual's discussion of crash responsibility, when a crash occurs in traffic:
choice_a: It is almost always entirely one driver's fault
choice_b: Most people involved can usually claim some responsibility for what took place
choice_c: The larger vehicle is always at fault
choice_d: Responsibility cannot be determined without a police report
explanation: In fact, most people involved in a crash can usually claim some responsibility for what took place -- neither party may have held up their end, even if one driver technically started the chain of events.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.8, 'Know Your Responsibilities'

question: To lessen the chances of a crash, the manual lists being visible, communicating your intentions, maintaining a space cushion, and:
choice_b: Searching your path of travel 12 seconds ahead
choice_c: Always riding faster than surrounding traffic
explanation: As a rider, you can't be sure others will see you or yield the right of way. To lessen your chances of a crash: be visible, communicate your intentions, maintain an adequate space cushion, and search your path of travel 12 seconds ahead.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.8, 'Know Your Responsibilities'

question: The manual states that control of a motorcycle -- direction, speed, and balance -- is best learned through:
choice_c: Practice, preferably in a formal course such as the PA Motorcycle Safety Program
choice_d: Trial and error in highway traffic
explanation: This manual cannot teach you how to control direction, speed, or balance -- that's something you can learn only through practice, preferably in a formal course of instruction like the PA Motorcycle Safety Program.
source_note: PennDOT Motorcycle Operator Manual (Pub 147, 11-24), p.8, 'Ride Within Your Abilities'
